title: Corvus and the Odd Bits Box
markdown:
On a speck of land no bigger than an enthusiastic kite lived Corvus, station master of the Littlest Lighthouse. Tidiness was his creed. The lighthouse was less a home than a museum of order, and he was its only curator.

Every day began with a feathered quill on crisp parchment. Sunrise: check. Foghorn: polished. Seashell collection: alphabetized by spiral complexity. List Item One: complete. Sandpipers whispered about those lists. Barnacles, who had nowhere to be, admired their neatness. He had even sorted his shiny pebbles by sparkle. Everyday Brights sat on a velvet cushion. Dull Companions lived in a sensible wooden box. The exceptional ones, which seemed to keep a private sun, had a place of honour. Even pebbles, in his world, needed a VIP section.

Then came a blustery Tuesday. Corvus was tidying the beach, distracted by a flock of raucous gulls arguing the finer points of fish etiquette, a subject he usually found delicious to ignore. His eye, trained on the exact angle of a wave’s retreat, caught something extraordinary: a large, remarkably shiny pebble, swirls of pearly white that shifted as he turned it, a faint rainbow sheen that promised sparkle. He tucked it into his satchel beneath a duller specimen and, in his head, filed it under Odd Bits and Bobs, the box he had invented for things that would not sit still in a category. Order, meeting its match, had built a drawer for disorder.

Because of that extra weight in the satchel, Rosa the hedgehog ambled up later, black nose twitching. Her burrow was a jumble of leaves and interesting twigs, but her memory was excellent.

"Corvus," she rumbled, like pebbles in surf, "have you seen my favourite sparkly shell? It was just here by the tide pools."

His slick black feathers felt ruffled from the inside. The pebble was not a pebble. It was her shell.

He spent the next hours in a flurry of private flapping. A butterfly of panic tried his ribs for a door. He had to replace the shell before she understood. He scoured sand and seaweed for a comparable gleam. Sea glass: too blue. A smooth grey stone: perfectly round and perfectly dull. Nothing shimmered the way her shell shimmered.

The weather joined in with all the subtlety of a runaway wave. Breeze became gale. Sand found his eyes. Rain arrived in fat drops, like ink spilled across his organized lists. The sea heaved, white-capped, no longer polite. Corvus was swept inland toward the lighthouse with Rosa paddling behind, little legs doing their best. They scrambled inside as a gust rattled the lantern room.

He looked at Rosa, fur plastered to her sides. He looked at the pearly shimmer on the Odd Bits and Bobs shelf. There was no more tidying this away.

The lighthouse beam swept its arc across the rain-lashed water. Corvus took a breath that tasted of salt. The wind tried to steal the words.

"Rosa," he said, "I have something to confess. I mistook your special shell for a pebble this morning. It is in my Odd Bits and Bobs box."

He gestured, weakly, at the shelf. Rosa nudged the shell with her nose. Cool pearl against whiskers.

"Well, Corvus," she said, a slow smile finding her snout, "it is a rather odd bit, isn’t it? Much more interesting than a pebble. Perhaps that box is exactly where it belongs. It found a collector who can see the sparkle."

The storm seemed to take the hint. Rain softened. The wind’s howl thinned to a whisper. Corvus felt cleaner than any surge had ever left him.

Ever since then his lists have kept a slightly whimsical extra line, and the Littlest Lighthouse, still impeccably orderly, keeps a shell on the odd-bits shelf that does not pretend to be a pebble.
characters: Corvus (tidy crow station master), Rosa (hedgehog friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
author: StoryGen Community
